headline: Stanford Scientists Reverse Coral Bleaching in Record 7 Weeks
meta_description: Breakthrough method restores ghostly white corals to full health through contact with healthy clones—offering new hope for reef restoration.
summary_short: Stanford researchers have reversed coral bleaching in just seven weeks using a groundbreaking method that transfers beneficial algae between corals.
body:
Corals bleached ghostly white and on the brink of death have been fully restored to health in seven weeks—the fastest recovery ever documented—through a simple method developed at Stanford University. When researchers placed bleached coral fragments in close contact with healthy clones from the same genetic colony, the tissues fused and beneficial algae flowed between them through microscopic channels, kickstarting recovery in as little as three days. The breakthrough, published in the journal Science Advances, reveals that bleached corals "are not dead yet," as lead researcher Danny Collins explains, and opens a new frontier for protecting reefs damaged by warming ocean temperatures.

The discovery began by accident in Professor Steve Palumbi's lab in 2025, when two coral fragments—one healthy and one bleached—tipped over in a tank and touched. Where they made contact, color returned. Collins realized that if harmful bacteria could transfer through contact, beneficial algae might too. His team tested the theory by arranging coral pairs close enough to touch while leaving gaps between control pairs. The results were decisive: corals in contact fully recovered within seven weeks, while those separated died.

What makes this finding truly remarkable is its speed and efficiency. After just five days of contact, bleached corals received enough algae to complete recovery independently. Once inside, the beneficial algae doubled every four days—roughly ten times faster than in wild corals. The team is now exploring ways to deliver algae without requiring continuous contact, potentially creating practical tools for large-scale reef restoration. As Professor Fiorenza Micheli notes, these insights "give us hope for the future" and may lead to the breakthrough needed to accelerate restoration of the world's threatened coral ecosystems.
quick_facts: Stanford lab restored bleached corals to full health in seven weeks—fastest recovery on record
Healthy coral clones transferred beneficial algae to bleached counterparts through tissue fusion
Recovery kickstarted in just three to five days of brief contact between coral fragments
Algae in bleached corals divided ten times faster than rates observed in wild corals
